newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS-Bass ponders Czech breweries merger.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bass ponders Czech breweries merger.

text.p: Britain's Bass Plc is considering an eventual mega-merger in the Czech brewing industry to compete against the big players in the European beer market, Bass's country manager in Prague said on Wednesday.

Bass, which already holds a 51 percent stake in Prague Breweries a.s., announced on Tuesday that it had increased its stake in another leading Czech brewer, Radegast a.s., to 33 percent from 20 percent.

Country manager Mervyn Childs told Reuters on Wednesday that a merger between two of the best known Czech brewers, which together control around 30 percent of the domestic market, would conform with Bass's desire to own a major Czech brewing group.
"In the medium to longer term ... we would like to consider a merger of Radegast and Prague Breweries group," he said.
"We've made no secret about our desire to be a substanial shareholder in a leading Czech brewing group...That group should have about 25 to 30 percent market share," he said.

Bass moved into the Czech beer market in 1993 when it took a 34 percent stake in Prague Breweries. The British group now also owns majority shares in two small regional Czech breweries, Vratislavice and Ostravar.
Apart from moving into the Czech market, which boasts the world's highest per capita beer consumption, Bass has been keen to push Czech beers in western Europe and Russia.
As a result, Prague Breweries, whose premium brand is Staropramen, has seen exports surge to 290,000 hectolitres in 1996 from 109,000 hectolitres in 1994.
"I really am convinced of the export opportunities for Czech beer but in an international sense you've got to be prepared. You're competing against your Heinekens and Carlsbergs," said Childs.

In announcing the increased equity stake in Radegast in a statement on Tuesday, Childs referred to the potential benefits in the export sphere of closer cooperation between Radegast and Prague breweries.

"We will wish to speak to both boards of directors about this as a priority ... It makes sense to combine the strengths and resources of both companies to compete more effectively in international markets."
Despite the strong export performance of Bass's current Czech holdings, Childs said on Wednesday that his ambitions were still far from being fulfilled.
"I'm more concerned about being the first Czech brewing company that exports one million hectolitres. That's the target. ... Once you've seen that we can grow from there."

A merger between Radegast and Prague Breweries will remain theoretical unless Bass can come to an agreement with Radegast's other major shareholders -- IPB group, which holds around 34 percent, and KIS a.s., which has around 23 percent.
"In the medium to longer term we would like to increase our (Radegast) stake but we'll do that hopefully through discussion and agreement with other major shareholders," said Childs.
